text.p: Ukraine's government has drawn up a 1997 budget calling for a fall in inflation and a lower budget deficit, but economists said on Tuesday it relies too heavily on printing new money and is over-optimistic on tax revenues.
The draft budget was approved at a cabinet meeting on Monday and is due to be presented to parliament this week, although it may be further amended before it reaches the legislature.
It provides for inflation of 25 percent, against forecasts of 45 percent for this year and a budget deficit of five percent of gross domestic product compared with 6.2 percent in 1996.
The 1997 deficit would be three percent, using Western methods of calculation.

"We are keeping to plans to strengthen financial discipline, help the Ukrainian producer and reduce excessive expenditure in working out the 1997 budget," said an official statement issued after the cabinet meeting.
But Western economists were unimpressed.

"There are two problem areas. One is that the budget calls for credits from the central bank of 2.5 billion hryvnia ($1.42 billion), more than 50 percent higher than last year," an economist with a Western advisory group familiar with the draft said.
"The other is that the revenue projections are very high."
Budget revenue, forecast at 45 percent of gross domestic product, was far too optimistic, he told Reuters.
"They will not get more than 38 percent of GDP, and even that is optimistic," he said. "There is no way that tax collection will reach that level."
But he said the projected 25 percent inflation rate for 1997 was realistic.
Ukraine has been under pressure to cut the deficit since the International Monetary Fund suspended payments on a loan in January after Kiev overshot spending targets.
A new $867 million standby credit was agreed in May.
This week's presentation of the budget marks Ukraine's first real attempt pass the budget in time. Budgets in the past have not been approved until well into the year they apply to.
Parliament, which is dominated by communists and their allies, is due to start consideration of the budget on Thursday, and to pass it by January 1.

The draft calls for a deficit of 6.07 billion hryvnia, to be covered by central bank credits of 2.5 billion hryvnia, 650 million hryvnia from Treasury bills and 2.09 billion hryvnia from other credits, the official Ukrinform news agency said.
Ministers say the biggest problem facing the government is a backlog of hundreds of millions of dollars in unpaid wages, expected to be made up as part of budget expenditure.
The tax system is undergoing reform to improve collection and make thresholds more realistic. Economists say up to 40 percent of economic activity takes place on the black market.

Rafal Antczak, economist at the Harvard Institute for International Development, said the draft did not represent a major departure from previous budgets, but it was was too early to comment, as it is likely to be amended substantially in parliament.
"This is very much a draft, a proposal to parliament," he said. "All I can say is there will be no radical changes (from previous budgets). It means continuity."
